Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
Keanu is a man who has spent his life in the sky, a place of order and control, yet he remains tethered to a single moment on the ground forty years ago. At 63, with the steady hands of a senior airline pilot, he presents as a man of immense capability, but his internal world is one of constant, quiet siege. The trauma occurred at dusk in a clearing in Vietnam. The air was thick with the rhythmic whump-whump-whump of the Huey's rotors as it descended to evacuate his platoon. They were taking casualties, and one of them was his friend. Keanu remembers the specific, rough texture of the canvas body bag under his palms as he helped lift it onto the chopper. It was coarse and unforgiving, and the memory of that tactile sensation has never left him.

For decades, Keanu managed. He built a family, a career, a life that looked successful from the outside. But the war came home with him in fragments. Any helicopter passing over his suburban home, whether for news or medical transport, can instantly dissolve the present. He will be standing at his kitchen window and suddenly, without warning, he is not a 63-year-old man looking at his garden but a terrified teenager in a jungle, the air tasting of cordite. When the memory hits, it brings with it the same raw terror he felt then, a physical wave of cold dread that makes his heart pound in his chest. He often describes this experience with a strange detachment, as if watching a film about someone else. "It feels like it belongs to another person," he has said, "a scared kid I don't know anymore." This sense of alienation from his own past has calcified into a core belief: there is something fundamentally wrong with him as a person.

His days are governed by a hypervigilance that has become second nature. Entering any new space, be it a pre-flight briefing room at the airport or a restaurant with his wife, Leilani, his first action is to locate every exit. He does it automatically, his eyes tracing the paths to safety before he can even process the room's occupants. He feels a constant, low-level hum of dread, a conviction that the world is an inherently dangerous place. This is most acute when others move unexpectedly. A flight attendant rushing down the aisle or a baggage handler making a sudden turn on the tarmac can cause him to flinch, his body tensing for an impact that never comes. The vigilance peaks as the sun begins to set. The specific quality of light at dusk, the same light that filled the sky during the evacuation, signals a shift in him. Night feels porous and unsafe, and he often finds himself awake for hours, listening to the house settle, certain that some threat lies just beyond the locked doors.

The routines of his job, once a source of pride, have become a landscape of potential triggers. The steady drone of his commercial jet is manageable, a world away from the sound of a Huey. But recently, while doing a walk-around inspection, his hand brushed against a canvas tool satchel left by a mechanic. The rough texture was identical to the body bag. The world tilted; the scent of jet fuel and concrete was replaced by jungle humidity and fear. He froze, unable to move, the full memory flooding him without permission. It was this incident, the momentary but total loss of control in his professional environment, that finally broke through his decades of stoicism. He feels he has lost the capacity for happiness he once had, replaced by a persistent, grey misery. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate fear of losing the last piece of his identity-the competent pilot-and a quiet, painful question of whether the happy man he remembers ever really existed at all.
